question: What is the difference between the null and blank field options?
reference_answer: null is database-related: if null=True, Django stores empty values as NULL in the database. blank is validation-related: if blank=True, form validation allows an empty value, and if blank=False the field is required. Both options default to False.
source_excerpt: null: If True, Django will store empty values as NULL in the database. Default is False. / blank: If True, the field is allowed to be blank. Default is False. / null is purely database-related, whereas blank is validation-related. If a field has blank=True, form validation will allow entry of an empty value. If a field has blank=False, the field will be required.

question: What is an abstract base class in Django model inheritance?
reference_answer: An abstract base class is a model with abstract = True in its Meta class that is used to put common information into several other models. It does not create a database table, has no manager and cannot be instantiated or saved directly. Its fields are added to each child model, so only one table per child model is created.
source_excerpt: You write your base class and put abstract=True in the Meta class. This model will then not be used to create any database table. Instead, when it is used as a base class for other models, its fields will be added to those of the child class. / It does not generate a database table or have a manager, and cannot be instantiated or saved directly.

question: What is a proxy model in Django?
reference_answer: A proxy model is declared with proxy = True in its Meta class and operates on the same database table as the original model. It is used to change only the Python behaviour of a model, for example to add methods or to change the default ordering or the default manager, without altering the original model. Data created through the proxy is saved as if the original model were used.
source_excerpt: Sometimes, however, you only want to change the Python behavior of a model – perhaps to change the default manager, or add a new method. This is what proxy model inheritance is for / You tell Django that it’s a proxy model by setting the proxy attribute of the Meta class to True. / The MyPerson class operates on the same database table as its parent Person class.

question: What is a handler in Django's logging system?
reference_answer: A handler is the engine that determines what happens to each message in a logger, for example writing it to the screen, to a file or to a network socket. Like loggers, handlers have a log level and ignore records whose level is lower. A logger can have several handlers with different log levels.
source_excerpt: The handler is the engine that determines what happens to each message in a logger. It describes a particular logging behavior, such as writing a message to the screen, to a file, or to a network socket. Like loggers, handlers also have a log level. / A logger can have multiple handlers, and each handler can have a different log level.

question: What is a URLconf in Django?
reference_answer: A URLconf (URL configuration) is a Python module that maps URL path expressions to Python functions, which are the views. Because it is pure Python code, it can be as short or as long as needed, can reference other mappings and can be constructed dynamically.
source_excerpt: To design URLs for an app, you create a Python module informally called a URLconf (URL configuration). This module is pure Python code and is a mapping between URL path expressions to Python functions (your views). This mapping can be as short or as long as needed. It can reference other mappings.

question: How do you tell Django to use the models of a new application?
reference_answer: Add the name of the module that contains the models.py file, for example "myapp", to the INSTALLED_APPS setting in the settings file. Then run manage.py migrate, optionally after creating migrations with manage.py makemigrations.
source_excerpt: Do this by editing your settings file and changing the INSTALLED_APPS setting to add the name of the module that contains your models.py. / When you add new apps to INSTALLED_APPS, be sure to run manage.py migrate, optionally making migrations for them first with manage.py makemigrations.

question: How do you define a many-to-many relationship between two models?
reference_answer: Use ManyToManyField as a class attribute of one model, with the related model class as the required positional argument, for example toppings = models.ManyToManyField(Topping) in the Pizza model. The field should be put in only one of the two models, generally in the model that is edited on a form, and a plural name is suggested.
source_excerpt: To define a many-to-many relationship, use ManyToManyField. You use it just like any other Field type: by including it as a class attribute of your model. ManyToManyField requires a positional argument: the class to which the model is related. / you should only put it in one of the models – not both. Generally, ManyToManyField instances should go in the object that’s going to be edited on a form.

question: How do you include another URLconf in a project's URL configuration?
reference_answer: Use include() inside path(), for example path("community/", include("aggregator.urls")). When Django encounters include(), it removes the part of the URL that has matched so far and sends the remaining string to the included URLconf. A list of path() instances can also be passed to include().
source_excerpt: path("community/", include("aggregator.urls")) / Whenever Django encounters include(), it chops off whatever part of the URL matched up to that point and sends the remaining string to the included URLconf for further processing. / Another possibility is to include additional URL patterns by using a list of path() instances.

question: How do you access setting values in your own Django code?
reference_answer: Import the object django.conf.settings (from django.conf import settings) and read its attributes, for example settings.DEBUG. Individual settings cannot be imported, because django.conf.settings is an object and not a module. Code should not import from global_settings or from the project's own settings file.

question: How can you pass extra arguments to a view function from the URLconf?
reference_answer: path() takes an optional third argument: a dictionary of extra keyword arguments that are passed to the view. For example, path("blog/<int:year>/", views.year_archive, {"foo": "bar"}) makes Django call views.year_archive(request, year=2005, foo='bar') for /blog/2005/. If a captured argument has the same name, the value from the dictionary is used.

question: Why does a request to /articles/2003 not match the URL pattern "articles/<int:year>/"?
reference_answer: Each of these URL patterns requires that the URL ends with a slash. The request /articles/2003 has no trailing slash, so it does not match any of the patterns.
source_excerpt: /articles/2003 would not match any of these patterns, because each pattern requires that the URL end with a slash.

question: Why does Django raise an error when a child model defines a field with the same name as a field in its parent model?
reference_answer: Django does not allow a model field inherited from a non-abstract base class to be overridden: if the base class has a field called author, no inheriting class can define a field or attribute called author. Overriding fields would cause problems, for example when initializing new instances and in serialization. Fields inherited from an abstract model are an exception and can be overridden or removed with None, and normal Python attributes can be overridden.
source_excerpt: If a non-abstract model base class has a field called author, you can’t create another model field or define an attribute called author in any class that inherits from that base class. This restriction doesn’t apply to model fields inherited from an abstract model. / Overriding fields in a parent model leads to difficulties in areas such as initializing new instances (specifying which field is being initialized in Model.__init__) and serialization.

question: Why do reverse name clashes occur when related_name is used in an abstract base class, and how can they be avoided?
reference_answer: The fields of an abstract base class are copied into every child class with exactly the same related_name and related_query_name, but these names must be unique. To avoid the problem, part of the value should contain '%(app_label)s' and '%(class)s', which are replaced by the lowercased name of the app and of the child class, so that each child gets a different name.
expected_section: Be careful with related_name and related_query_name
source_excerpt: you must always specify a unique reverse name and query name for the field. This would normally cause a problem in abstract base classes, since the fields on this class are included into each of the child classes, with exactly the same values / part of the value should contain '%(app_label)s' and '%(class)s'.

question: Why does Django raise an ImportError or a RuntimeError about settings in a standalone script?
reference_answer: If DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE is not set and configure() is not called, Django raises an ImportError the first time a setting is accessed. If DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE is set, settings are accessed and configure() is called afterwards, Django raises a RuntimeError because the settings have already been configured. Exactly one of configure() or DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE must be used.
expected_section: Either configure() or DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE is required
source_excerpt: If you don’t set DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE and don’t call configure(), Django will raise an ImportError exception the first time a setting is accessed. If you set DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE, access settings values somehow, then call configure(), Django will raise a RuntimeError / Use exactly one of either configure() or DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE. Not both, and not neither.

question: Why does a Django site stop working after DEBUG is set to False?
reference_answer: When DEBUG = False, Django does not work at all without a suitable value for ALLOWED_HOSTS. This setting protects the site against some CSRF attacks. If a wildcard is used, the Host header must be validated separately, and the web server in front of Django should also validate the host.

question: How should the SECRET_KEY setting be handled in production?
reference_answer: The secret key must be a large random value and must be kept secret. It should not be used anywhere else or committed to source control; instead of hardcoding it, it can be loaded from an environment variable or from a file. When keys are rotated, old keys can be placed in SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS and should be removed from there in a timely manner.
source_excerpt: The secret key must be a large random value and it must be kept secret. Make sure that the key used in production isn’t used anywhere else and avoid committing it to source control. / consider loading it from an environment variable / If rotating secret keys, you may use SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS / Ensure that old secret keys are removed from SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS in a timely manner.

question: What does the CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE setting do in a production deployment?
reference_answer: Setting CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE to True prevents the CSRF cookie from being transmitted over HTTP by accident, so that it is only sent over HTTPS.
source_excerpt: Set this to True to avoid transmitting the CSRF cookie over HTTP accidentally.

question: What is the benefit of enabling persistent database connections with CONN_MAX_AGE?
reference_answer: Persistent database connections can give a noticeable speed-up when connecting to the database takes a significant part of the request processing time. This helps especially on virtualized hosts with limited network performance.
source_excerpt: Enabling persistent database connections can result in a nice speed-up when connecting to the database accounts for a significant part of the request processing time. This helps a lot on virtualized hosts with limited network performance.

question: Can settings be changed while a Django application is running?
reference_answer: No. Settings should not be altered at runtime, for example by assigning settings.DEBUG = True in a view. The only place where settings should be assigned is a settings file.
source_excerpt: You shouldn’t alter settings in your applications at runtime. For example, don’t do this in a view: settings.DEBUG = True # Don't do this! The only place you should assign to settings is in a settings file.

question: Which settings define who is notified by email about server errors and broken links?
reference_answer: ADMINS are notified of 500 errors by email and MANAGERS are notified of 404 errors. IGNORABLE_404_URLS can be used to filter out spurious reports. Because error reporting by email does not scale well, an error monitoring system such as Sentry can be considered.

question: How do you define a one-to-one relationship with OneToOneField?
reference_answer: Use OneToOneField as a class attribute of the model, with the related model class as the required positional argument, for example a Restaurant model with a OneToOneField to Place. It is most useful on the primary key of an object that extends another object. It accepts an optional parent_link argument and no longer automatically becomes the primary key, so a model can have several OneToOneFields.
source_excerpt: To define a one-to-one relationship, use OneToOneField. You use it just like any other Field type: by including it as a class attribute of your model. This is most useful on the primary key of an object when that object “extends” another object in some way. OneToOneField requires a positional argument / OneToOneField fields also accept an optional parent_link argument.

question: How do you add custom methods such as __str__() and get_absolute_url() to a model?
reference_answer: Custom methods are defined on the model class and add row-level functionality that acts on a particular instance. __str__() returns the string representation of an object, which is used for example in the interactive console and in the admin, and should almost always be defined. get_absolute_url() tells Django how to calculate the URL for an object and is used, for example, in the admin interface.

question: How does Django resolve a namespaced URL such as 'polls:index' when reverse() is called?
reference_answer: Django splits the name and first looks for a matching application namespace ('polls'). If a current application is defined, for example with the current_app argument of reverse(), its URL resolver is used; otherwise the default application instance is used, and if there is none, the last deployed instance. If the namespace does not match an application namespace, Django tries it as an instance namespace, repeats this for nested namespaces and finally resolves the view name.
source_excerpt: First, Django looks for a matching application namespace / The current application can be specified with the current_app argument to the reverse() function. / If there is no current application, Django looks for a default application instance. / If there is no default application instance, Django will pick the last deployed instance of the application / Django will attempt a direct lookup of the namespace as an instance namespace.

question: How can the same view be used for a URL pattern that captures a value and one that does not?
reference_answer: Give the view argument a default value, for example def page(request, num=1), and point two path() patterns to the same view: path("blog/", views.page) and path("blog/page<int:num>/", views.page). If the first pattern matches, the default value 1 is used; if the second matches, the captured num value is used.
source_excerpt: path("blog/", views.page), path("blog/page<int:num>/", views.page) / def page(request, num=1): / If the first pattern matches, the page() function will use its default argument for num, 1. If the second pattern matches, page() will use whatever num value was captured.

question: How is settings.configure() used to configure Django without DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE?
reference_answer: Call django.conf.settings.configure() with keyword arguments for the settings, for example settings.configure(DEBUG=True). Each argument name is an uppercase setting name; settings that are not passed use their default values. This is mostly used when a part of Django, such as the template system, is used inside a larger application.
